You are being evaluated on Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream of ARC-style grid puzzles.
Each puzzle instance has a task id and a test input grid. Tasks recur across the
stream with fresh inputs. Each instance is a separate conversation: the next one
starts without this one's messages.

On every message you must choose exactly one action and put it as a JSON object
on the last line of your reply:
  {"action": "submit", "grid": [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5]]}   submit an output grid
  {"action": "request_demos"}                            ask for one more demonstration pair for this task
  {"action": "finish"}                                   end the instance, once it is over
Grids are lists of rows; cells are integers 0-9; dimensions are 1-30.

Each demo request returns one more input-output pair of the task, up to the demo cap shown
with the input.

Scoring: every wrong submission costs 1 and every demo request costs 1. An
instance is over when a submission is correct or when the attempt cap is reached, and
reaching the cap is charged the full cap. Feedback on a submission is only
correct/incorrect. There is no way to abandon an instance, and finish is refused until
the instance is over. Each instance is scored on its own, and lower cost is better.

# Continual-ARC inference and interaction

Use for interactive Continual-ARC instances with a test grid, demonstration requests, and scored submissions.

## Protocol first

- On every turn, provide exactly one action JSON object on the last line: `{"action":"submit","grid":[...]}`, `{"action":"request_demos"}`, or `{"action":"finish"}`. Do not add prose or unrelated tool calls to puzzle turns.
- `finish` is only appropriate after the instance is over. Keep dimensions and cell values valid (rows/columns 1–30, values 0–9).
- Demonstration requests and wrong submissions have explicit costs. Use received evidence carefully; request another demo when it can resolve genuine ambiguity, rather than reflexively requesting or guessing.

## Infer from observed differences

1. Parse the entire input/output demo pair and identify exact cell changes, objects, colors, and spatial relationships. Distinguish unchanged elements from transformed ones.
2. Compare multiple demonstrations when available. Prefer the narrowest rule that explains all examples, including which components are preserved and how edge cases behave.
3. Do not assume a loaded ARC skill applies just because it is familiar; use its rule only when the observed demo supports it. In particular, do not infer stamping from a grid containing compact colored shapes and markers alone.
4. When the rule is underdetermined, request a demo specifically to distinguish plausible hypotheses. Avoid a low-information demo if a confident rule is already established.
5. Apply the inferred transformation to the test grid, preserving everything not implicated by the rule. Validate dimensions, row lengths, and that each changed cell follows the inferred rule before submitting.

## Pitfalls

- Treat the whole grid as evidence: templates, isolated markers, large patterns, and background may have different roles. A compact shape may be a distractor or part of some other relation.
- A single demo can leave the changed object or mapping unclear; compare input and output directly rather than relying on visual intuition.
- Keep output to the required action JSON. name: continual-arc-template-stamping
description: Use when ARC shows a template object and scattered markers.
---

# ARC template stamping

Use this when a demo shows a distinctive compact colored object and many single-cell markers on a background, and the output repeats the object around each marker.

1. Identify the background, source template, and marker color by comparing demo input/output. The source template is usually a small rectangular pattern whose background-colored cells are transparent.
2. Determine the anchor cell of the template from the demonstration: commonly a central template cell maps onto each marker. Verify this using multiple markers, including edge markers.
3. For each marker in the test grid, copy the template's non-background cells with the same relative offsets, centered/aligned on the marker; replace the marker as part of the stamp. Preserve unrelated background and the original source object unless the demonstration shows otherwise.
4. If stamps overlap, infer precedence from the demo and apply consistently. Keep grid dimensions unchanged; clip only if edge behavior is demonstrated.
5. A related rule (validated in task-e6f5b2c7): when the seed is a compact shape of color C on background B, use the shape's full bounding box and its C-cell mask. Scan same-sized windows for the marker/background value at every mask position; if a demo confirms mask-only matching, non-mask cells may be arbitrary and must not be constrained. Recolor the matched mask cells with C, preserving all other cells and the original seed. Add a non-mask constraint only when the demo clearly establishes one. Verify on the demo before applying; do not confuse this with recoloring arbitrary long background runs.

Validated mask-only variant (task-e6f5b2c7): the 5-colored seed mask in its 5x4 bounding box had relative cells `{(0,2),(1,1),(2,1),(2,2),(3,0),(3,1),(4,2),(4,3)}` (0-indexed). The demonstration showed the same shape stamped at windows whose mask cells were all 0, with arbitrary values at non-mask cells. The 25x13 test likewise had exactly two such placements, anchored at `(2,1)` and `(12,1)` (0-indexed); recolor only those mask cells to 5 and preserve the seed and all other cells. Requiring non-mask cells to be non-background wrongly excludes these validated matches. This signature can recur as a compact colored template with scattered exact mask-color/marker locations.

Validated additional seed-mask rule (task-e6f5b2c7): background 9, template color 4. The 4-mask is the L triomino in a 2x2 bounding box, relative coordinates `{(0,1),(1,0),(1,1)}` (top-right, bottom-left, bottom-right; equivalently all except top-left). In the demo, all-zero matches of this three-cell mask were changed to 4, preserving all other cells, including arbitrary values at the non-mask/top-left position. For the test with background 6 and template 8 (seed at rows 2–3, cols 6–7), find every 2x2 window where cells at offsets `(0,1),(1,0),(1,1)` are 0 and recolor those three cells to 8; top-left is unconstrained and unchanged. A single scan of 2x2 anchors in the demonstrated 29x11 test yielded anchors `(1,4),(3,0),(5,1),(6,1),(6,5),(7,0),(7,1),(8,0),(10,7),(13,6),(13,7),(14,3),(14,4),(14,5),(14,6),(15,3),(16,6),(16,7),(17,6),(17,7),(18,4),(20,2),(22,2),(22,8),(26,5)` (0-indexed). Keep the source seed unchanged.

6. Another distinct rule (demonstrated repeatedly in task-63fa1523): color the background cells inside closed regions outlined by a connected line pattern in another color; the fill color is 4 in those demos. Preserve the outline and all exterior cells. A further validated variant has multiple closed, irregular/thick-outline pockets on the same grid (background 3, outline 6): fill every enclosed interior cell with 4, independently, preserving both outlines and the exterior. This confirms the rule applies to each connected closed pocket, not only one rectangle or one pocket touching the grid boundary. Crucial edge case: a region can touch a grid edge and still be enclosed by outline segments plus the grid border. Do NOT seed flood fill from every background cell along the grid edge—this incorrectly labels such an enclosed region as exterior. Instead, treat the four grid corners as exterior seeds, flood-fill the background color through 4-neighbor cells, and recolor unvisited background components. In the test, this correctly filled the complete 4-row-by-3-column region at rows 5–8, columns 22–24, which touches the right edge but is separated from the outside by the outline; regions connected to the grid corners stayed unchanged. Always recolor the entire enclosed component, not just its central-looking cells, and validate all dimensions. The earlier attempt that colored extra top/bottom/right background was wrong; the later attempt that filled only columns 22–23 missed the component’s third column. For this geometry, a compact background pocket connected to no corner is the signal—even if it includes edge cells.

Verified additional example from task-63fa1523: a 7-colored closed rectangular outline on a 5 background marks a pocket to recolor 4, preserving the outline and all exterior cells. In the test, the 5×5 outline at rows 2–6 and columns 0–4 encloses the 3×3 interior at rows 3–5, columns 1–3; all nine interior cells become 4. The demo confirms that all cells of enclosed background components are filled (not only visually central cells), and unrelated/background exterior components stay unchanged.

Worked pattern from task-76eceeef: a 3x3 template with rows `[bg,5,5]`, `[8,5,8]`, `[8,5,0]` is centered on each marker cell (color 1), replacing each marker; the seed template remains. A separate demo used a vertical 8/1/1 stamp at each color-3 marker. The demo establishes template shape, anchor, and whether to preserve the original seed.

## Distinguish unrelated selective-recolor tasks
Do not apply template-stamping logic merely because a grid contains bars and scattered colored objects. In task-c08d69dc demonstrations, outputs selectively recolored existing components, with mappings varying by example (observed examples included 7→2, 5→6, 6→1, 1→2, 1→5, 8→2, and 6→0); no fixed color mapping or stamping rule was established. The test was not solved. For similar scenes, derive the structural selection/color relationship from multiple input-output differences before changing any cells; preserve everything else. {"success": true, "name": "continual-arc-inference", "file": "references/edge-boundaries.md", "content": "# Edge-touching boundaries in fill tasks

This session exposed a recurring validation issue for region-filling puzzles. Demos showed that the fill target can be fully contained by a boundary that touches the canvas border. A flood fill which seeds all background cells along the grid edge then treats the target as exterior, even though the demos establish it as an enclosed cavity.

## Reliable analysis

1. Compare demo input/output cell-by-cell and record the exact changed coordinates. Identify the connected outline and each altered component, including whether a component touches a grid edge.
2. Verify the rule against all available examples before transferring it to a differently shaped test. Do not infer that every background component adjacent to an edge should be filled.
3. For each candidate target, identify a closed perimeter in the actual geometry. The canvas frame may complete part of that perimeter only if the demos demonstrate that edge-touching cavities are filled.
4. A border-seeded flood fill is useful for cavities fully enclosed by grid cells, but is not sufficient when the grid edge itself participates in a demonstrated enclosure. Either model the perimeter-plus-frame explicitly or classify candidate regions by their demonstrated outline relationship.
5. Preserve the outline and all unrelated cells. Validate exact row count, width, and changed coordinates before submission.

## Pitfall from this interaction

The test contained an irregular outline touching the lower and left edges and a vertical segment near the right side. A guessed set of edge-adjacent rectangles was submitted without a full demo-validated perimeter analysis and was incorrect. The reliable lesson is not a specific fill mask: it is to use the demos to determine exactly which boundary geometry qualifies and avoid hand-selecting rectangles. The full demos and test from this session remain in the conversation transcript; no unverified test output is asserted here.
